extracted.intended_audience: students and readers studying classical (Greek & Roman) literature; attendees of a lecture course on classical literature (Schlegel)
extracted.subtask_description: A study-question guide for analysing Greek and Roman literature (origins, periodization, authors, styles, philosophy, and the relation of literature to politics and society). It frames the topics and critical dimensions to be considered in lectures or close-reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course structure and ordering of topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Which has precedence in the order of time — What is his principal object — What does he propose to examine with reference to the northern literature — What will be the next topic? Crusades, &c. — What will form the last part of the course?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides planning and sequencing of a lecture/course: choose chronological precedence, define principal object, relate southern classical topics to 'northern' literature, and set successive lecture topics and concluding material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of principal object and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: What is his principal object? — Does he intimate that he will offer any new critical opinions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear articulation of the critic/lecturer's aims and whether new critical claims or reinterpretations will be advanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and external influences on Greek literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Whence came their alphabet? — Their old traditions and poems — Did they receive much from this source? — How did they appropriate it? — How were Ante-Homeric poems probably related to the Asiatic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate provenance of literary forms (alphabet, traditions), degree of foreign influences (Asiatic/Eastern), and processes of appropriation and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of cultural independence and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: In what respect were the Greeks independent? — How was it with the Romans? — The modern Europeans? — Have they improved their possession? — When?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how much a culture innovates vs inherits: independence of Greeks versus Romans/moderns and subsequent improvement or loss over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodization of literary history
rubrics_metrics.description: How is the Greek history divided? — When does the proper epoch of Grecian literature begin? — What commences with Solon? — What period of Grecian history does he pass over?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear chronological divisions and identification of key turning points (e.g., Solon, heroic age, Alexandrian age) when evaluating development and character of literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of major historical events on literature
rubrics_metrics.description: What would have been the effect of the Greeks failing in the war with Persia? — What was the effect of the last event? — What threatened Greece at this time? — How did political change affect literature?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how wars, conquests, political shifts (e.g., Persian wars, loss of independence) alter literary production, taste, and preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and composition of early narrative songs and Homeric poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: What was the previous state of things? — What traditions had the Greeks? — Why are the songs of narrative important? — What is the most valuable portion of early Greek poetry? — How were they composed, and when?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate importance, age, composition methods, and cultural function of oral/narrative songs and the relative value of their surviving portions (e.g., Homeric corpus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historicity vs literary value of heroic traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Does Schlegel express doubt of the actual occurrence of the Trojan war? — Is the story of Helen probable? — What remains confirm the traditions? — Was it of much consequence whether the story were true or not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between factual historicity and literary/cultural significance; assess whether truth affects poetic or cultural value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative assessment of poetic traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: In what respects are the Homeric poems superior to the old songs of the Arabians, and the poems of Ossian? — In what respects are the Homeric poems excelled by those of the north? — In what does their peculiar excellence lie?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare stylistic, thematic, and cultural strengths/weaknesses across traditions (Homeric vs northern/Oriental/modern imitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of epic heroes and their poetic function
rubrics_metrics.description: What do Achilles and Ulysses represent? — Describe Achilles. — Describe Ulysses. — What advantage does such a hero give the poet?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how hero-types embody cultural ideals and serve narrative/poetic purposes; evaluate their utility to the poet in shaping theme and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship, naming, and identity questions (Homer)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is said about Homer's name? — What is Homer to us? — What is the other explanation of his name? — Which is preferred?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider authorship attribution, names, and the interpretive implications of different theories about a canonical author's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of critical attention
rubrics_metrics.description: To what class of writers does he propose to confine his attention? — What will he pass over? — What period of Grecian history does he pass over? — With what was it occupied?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define explicit topical and chronological boundaries for study; justify exclusions and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating lyric poetry (Pindar) — obscurity and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: What are Pindar's characteristics? — In what respect is Pindar peculiarly valuable? — Are the modern imitations of Pindar successful? — What makes Pindar obscure?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lyric qualities, thematic range, cultural specificity, reasons for obscurity, and challenges for imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and classification of historical writing (Herodotus vs Thucydides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Who was Herodotus? — What is the character of his work? — What is the nature of his episodes? — Why is his work called epic? — Why is it more properly a history? — Of what was Thucydides the inventor? — What are the characteristics of his method?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate historical method, narrative scope, episodic character, and innovations in historiography; compare literary and analytic approaches of different historians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic form and the role of chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: From what did the Greek tragedy arise? — In what respect is perfect harmony required? — Who exhibited it? — To what purpose did Euripides turn the chorus? — What are the beauties of Euripides's choruses? — How does want of harmony affect his plays?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dramatic structure, the function of chorus, requirements for harmony between parts, and how departures affect dramatic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's social function and limits (Aristophanes)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the subject of Aristophanes? — In what points are his plays valuable? — What is requisite to judge of his merits? — What fault is found with modern literature? — How are his poems defiled? — What makes much of his wit unintelligible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comic genre in cultural context, required historical knowledge for appreciation, boundaries of license, and issues of coarse/obscene material versus lasting merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of sophists and the intellectual climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the influence of the sophists salutary? — What were injured by sophistry? — What was done by Socrates? — How did sophistry treat the popular belief and morality? — What was the political effect of these doctrines?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pedagogical methods, ethical/political consequences, and how sophistic rhetoric shaped literary culture and public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers' relation to poetry and mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: How did the more ancient Greek Philosophers treat Homer and Hesiod? — How did the philosophers regard all poetry? — Had the philosophers inquired into the nature of Deity? — How were the representations of the gods viewed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine philosophical critiques of myth and poetry, tensions between poetic tradition and philosophical inquiry, and implications for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical content across poets (materialism, theology)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the philosophical character of the Theogony? — In what part of Homer does philosophical materialism chiefly appear? — What is the weakest part of Homer's productions? — Which are most interesting, his gods or his men?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate underlying metaphysical/ontological views in poetic texts and judge which elements (divine vs human) carry greatest interest or weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as symbolic or hidden meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Had the mythology of the Greeks any hidden meaning? — How is the fable of Saturn or Chronos explained? — Are there other representations of this kind in Hesiod?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider allegorical or cosmological readings of myth and the degree to which myths encode symbolic explanations of natural or moral phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay between visual arts (sculpture) and poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: What people brought sculpture to the greatest perfection? — Why? — What is remarked of their poetry? — Was their sculpture more refined than their poetry? — Of what do we always find traces in the representations of the poets?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze cross-art influences: how visual aesthetics inform poetic description and cultural valuation of different arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and regional loci of philosophical and poetic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Where did the poetry and philosophy of the ancients originate? — Who were the earliest poets and philosophers? — Who taught philosophy in Magna Grecia and among the southern Italians? — Where does the genius of the Greeks appear most rich and inventive?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace geographic and cultural sources of intellectual innovation and how location shaped philosophical and poetic developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materialist and atomistic doctrines and their cultural effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Who reduced the atomical philosophy to a regular system? — Who made it prevalent among the Greeks and Romans? — What does it strike at the root of? — Had these doctrines any practical effect? — What appears to have been preserved in the mysteries?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the social and religious implications of materialist philosophies: their threat to popular faith, effect on doctrines like immortality, and survival of ideas in mystery cults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy and exercises of sophists
rubrics_metrics.description: How did one of the sophists commence his instructions? — Whom did they educate? — What did they teach young men to do? — What did they propose by way of exercise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate teaching methods, curricula, rhetorical exercises, and their intended social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major philosophical systems: Plato vs Aristotle
rubrics_metrics.description: Who were the two greatest masters of Grecian philosophy? — Explain their different characteristics. — What is the great leading principle of Plato? — How does Aristotle define virtue? — What is the fundamental idea of Aristotle's philosophy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare foundational epistemology/metaphysics, methods, strengths, and faults of major philosophers to assess their influence on literature, art, and science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation, adaptation, and limits of transplanting national legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Can the heroic legends of one country be adopted by another? — What is the rule with respect to the imitation of dramatic poetry? — Should its form be imitated? — Where is imitation most hurtful? — What was the practice of the Roman lyrical poets?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess when imitation is appropriate or harmful: consider cultural rootedness of legends, suitability of forms, and risks in transplanting national heroics or dramatic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical use of nature and subject-matter selection
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the poetry of nature? — How should the poet treat natural philosophy? — Should he explain scientific causes? — What is the business of the poet with respect to natural philosophy? — Why does a poet love solitude?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate modes by which poets incorporate nature/science: didactic explanation vs evocative presentation, and the poet's imaginative liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline of poetry and characteristics of learned/didactic verse
rubrics_metrics.description: What happens to poetry in its decline? — What subjects does he pronounce unpoetical? — What is the fault of the learned poetry of the Alexandrians? — What was the design of the early Greeks in their didactic poetry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify markers of poetic decline (overlearned subject matter, loss of imaginative power) and critique the effects of didacticism on poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman literature: imitation, national character, and original contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the Romans borrow everything from Greece? — What did the influence of Greek authors and manners make them forget? — What were the subjects of the old Roman ballads? — What is said of Ennius, Lucretius, Virgil, Horace?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Roman balancing of imitation and originality: retention/loss of indigenous forms (ballads), success of adaptations, and assessment of major Roman poets' national suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a suitable historical subject for an epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Is a historical event a proper basis for a heroic poem? — Does it need to be a remote event? — What is more important? — What should be the nature of the historical event which is to form the basis of a heroic poem?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set criteria for epic subjects: remoteness vs thematic suitability, moral/aesthetic grandeur, and the event's capacity to sustain heroic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, style, and purity as evaluative dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: In what three authors is the utmost purity and perfection of the Roman language displayed? — What are their respective merits? — What is said of Tacitus' style? — How is Cicero characterized?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge authors by linguistic purity, stylistic excellence, rhetorical skill, and how these qualities relate to intellectual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions necessary for literary flourishing (patronage, education, institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Scipios began to patronize Greek literature and rhetoric, what did Rome possess? — What was done by Cato? — By Ennius? — What is necessary to complete the idea of a flourishing literature? — How long did the classical period of Roman literature last?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutional supports (patronage, education, civic structures) and key figures as prerequisites for a mature literary culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political structures' influence on literary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: What was necessary to the intellectual greatness of Athens? — For what was Sparta remarkable? — What was the tendency of her municipal system? — Wherein consists the peculiar merit of Caesar or Cicero? — What idea animates all the Roman writers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how political life (republican vs municipal structures, civic ideals) shapes national literary genres, themes, and authorial temperaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late antique literature and religious/intellectual contest
rubrics_metrics.description: What evinces the growth of infidelity? — What is shown in the works of Sextus Empiricus? — What was the effect of oriental opinions? — What was the character of the contest with Christianity? — What three preliminaries are necessary to give any satisfactory idea of this contest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate late antique intellectual conflicts (pagan philosophies vs Christianity), cultural exchange with Eastern doctrines, and their literary consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential elements of poetry (essence and ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the peculiar sphere of poetry? — What is a second end of poetry? — In what three things does the essence of all poetry consist? — Can poetry consist entirely in representations of actual life? — Can one write poetry without inventive power?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set evaluative criteria for poetry: imaginative/inventive power, representation of life, higher purposes beyond mere mimesis, and balance of elements that constitute poetic essence.
